name: Leonardo da Vinci
info: Leonardo di ser Piero da Vinci was an Italian painter, draughtsman, engineer and scientist of the High Renaissance, who worked in Florence, Milan, Rome and France and is remembered for the Mona Lisa, The Last Supper and his notebooks.

facts.born: 15 April 1452 in or close to Vinci, a Tuscan hill town about 35 kilometres from Florence; born out of wedlock to Ser Piero da Vinci, a Florentine notary, and Caterina di Meo Lippi, of the lower class
facts.died: 2 May 1519 at the manor house of Clos Lucé, near the Château d'Amboise in France, at the age of 67, possibly of a stroke
facts.role: Master in the Guild of Saint Luke in Florence from 1472; in the service of Ludovico Sforza in Milan, 1482–1499; military architect and engineer to Cesare Borgia, 1502; in Rome, 1513–1516; in the service of King Francis I of France from 1516
facts.known: the Mona Lisa; The Last Supper; the Virgin of the Rocks; the Vitruvian Man drawing; some 13,000 pages of notes and drawings; anatomical drawings made from dissections; designs for flying machines and other devices; the shading technique called sfumato

t: Born out of wedlock near Florence and trained in the workshop of Andrea del Verrocchio, Leonardo made his career at the courts of Milan, Florence, Rome and France as a painter, engineer and deviser of pageants.

Fewer than 25 major works are attributed to him, several of them unfinished or ruined by his own experiments in technique, yet the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper are among the most famous and most reproduced paintings in the Western canon.
His notebooks record discoveries in anatomy, hydrodynamics, geology, optics and friction, but he did not publish them, and they had little to no direct influence on later science.
dyk: Most of Leonardo's writings are in mirror-image cursive. He wrote with his left hand, and it was probably easier for him to write from right to left.
ev: Leonardo is born in or close to Vinci in Tuscany, the son of the notary Ser Piero da Vinci and Caterina di Meo Lippi
At the age of 20 he qualifies as a master in the Guild of Saint Luke in Florence, while continuing to work with Verrocchio
He leaves Florence for Milan and the court of Ludovico Sforza, where he works until 1499
He paints The Last Supper for the refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan
He enters the service of Cesare Borgia as military architect and engineer and draws a town plan of Imola
Back in Florence, he begins a portrait of Lisa del Giocondo, the Mona Lisa, on which he works into his later years
He enters the service of King Francis I of France and is given the use of the manor house of Clos Lucé
Leonardo dies at Clos Lucé at the age of 67 and is buried at the Château d'Amboise

sections.early:
Leonardo di ser Piero da Vinci was born on 15 April 1452 in, or close to, the Tuscan hill town of Vinci, about 35 kilometres from Florence. He was born out of wedlock to Caterina di Meo Lippi, a woman of the lower class, and Ser Piero da Vinci, a Florentine legal notary and landowner descended from a long line of notaries. Where he was born remains uncertain; a local oral tradition names the hamlet of Anchiano. Both parents married other people the year after his birth, and from his father's four marriages Leonardo eventually had 16 half-siblings, all much younger, with whom he had very little contact.

Very little is known about his childhood, and much is shrouded in myth, partly because of the frequently apocryphal biography by the 16th-century art historian Giorgio Vasari. Tax records show that by at least 1457 he lived in the household of his paternal grandfather, Antonio da Vinci. He received only a basic and informal education in vernacular writing, reading and mathematics.

In the mid-1460s the family moved to Florence, then the centre of Christian Humanist thought and culture. Around the age of 14 Leonardo became a garzone, or studio boy, in the workshop of Andrea del Verrocchio, the leading Florentine painter and sculptor of his time; he was an apprentice by 17 and remained in training for seven years. The workshop, with which Ghirlandaio, Perugino and Botticelli were also associated, taught drafting, chemistry, metallurgy, plaster casting, mechanics and woodwork as well as drawing, painting, sculpting and modelling.
sections.rise:
By 1472, at the age of 20, Leonardo qualified as a master in the Guild of Saint Luke, the guild of artists and doctors of medicine, though he continued to collaborate and live with Verrocchio even after his father set him up in his own workshop. His earliest known dated work is a pen-and-ink drawing of the Arno valley of 1473. In January 1478 he received an independent commission for an altarpiece for the Chapel of Saint Bernard in the Palazzo della Signoria, and in March 1481 the monks of San Donato in Scopeto commissioned The Adoration of the Magi. Neither was completed.

In 1482 Leonardo went to Milan, sent, by one account, by Lorenzo de' Medici to Ludovico Sforza, known as il Moro, who ruled the city between 1479 and 1499. He wrote Sforza a letter describing what he could achieve in engineering and weapon design, and mentioned that he could paint. He worked in Milan until 1499. There he was commissioned to paint the Virgin of the Rocks for the Confraternity of the Immaculate Conception and The Last Supper for the monastery of Santa Maria delle Grazie, prepared floats and pageants for the court, and made a model for the cupola of Milan Cathedral.

His largest project for Sforza was an equestrian monument to Ludovico's predecessor, Francesco Sforza, known as the Gran Cavallo, which would have surpassed in size the two large equestrian statues of the Renaissance by Donatello and Verrocchio. Leonardo completed a model of the horse and detailed plans for its casting. By the 1490s he had already been described as a "Divine" painter.
sections.deeds:
The Last Supper, painted in the 1490s, shows the moment when Jesus has just said that one of his disciples will betray him; it was acclaimed as a masterpiece of design and characterisation. After the fall of Sforza, Leonardo worked in Venice as a military architect, returned to Florence, and in 1502 entered the service of Cesare Borgia, son of Pope Alexander VI, for whom he drew a town plan of Imola. By October 1503 he had begun a portrait of Lisa del Giocondo, the Mona Lisa, whose shadowed modelling came to be called sfumato. He also designed a mural of The Battle of Anghiari for the Florentine Signoria, with Michelangelo assigned the opposite wall. From 1506 he was again in Milan, under its French governor.

Alongside the paintings he kept notebooks throughout his life: some 13,000 pages of notes and drawings on painting, anatomy, plants, rock formations, whirlpools, war machines, flying machines and architecture. Given permission to dissect human corpses at hospitals in Florence, Milan and Rome, he made more than 240 detailed anatomical drawings, among them one of the first scientific drawings of a foetus in utero, and was the first to define atherosclerosis and liver cirrhosis.

He was valued in his lifetime as an engineer. His journals contain designs for a flapping ornithopter and a machine with a helical rotor, hydraulic pumps, a mechanical knight and a steam cannon, and in 1493 he first stated the laws of sliding friction, which were not rediscovered until 1699. His approach to science was observational: he described and depicted a phenomenon in the utmost detail.
sections.opponents:
Much of what Leonardo began was not finished, or did not last. His first two independent commissions in Florence were abandoned when he left for Milan. In November 1494 Ludovico Sforza gave the metal intended for the Gran Cavallo to his brother-in-law for a cannon to defend the city against Charles VIII of France. For The Last Supper Leonardo used tempera over a ground that was mainly gesso instead of the reliable technique of fresco; the surface was subject to mould and flaking, and within a hundred years one viewer described the painting as "completely ruined". The Battle of Anghiari also deteriorated rapidly and is known from a copy by Rubens. The prior of Santa Maria delle Grazie hounded him over his irregular hours of work, and in Rome the pope cancelled a painting commission when the artist set about developing a new kind of varnish.

Court records show that in 1476 he and three other young men were charged with sodomy; the charges were dismissed for lack of evidence. His assistant Salaì, whom he called "a thief, a liar, stubborn, and a glutton", stayed in his household for thirty years.

As a scientist he was mostly ignored by the scholars of his day, since he lacked formal education in Latin and mathematics, and he did not publish his findings. Research by Marc van den Broek has found older prototypes for more than 100 inventions ascribed to him, suggesting that a large portion had been conceived before his lifetime. Vasari has him lament on his deathbed that he had "offended against God and men by failing to practice his art as he should have done".
sections.last:
In September 1513 Leonardo went to Rome, where Giovanni de' Medici had become pope as Leo X, and until 1516 he spent much of his time living in the Belvedere Courtyard of the Apostolic Palace. He practised botany in the Vatican Gardens, made plans for draining the Pontine Marshes and dissected cadavers. He became ill there, in what may have been the first of multiple strokes.

After King Francis I of France recaptured Milan in October 1515, Leonardo was invited to France and entered the king's service in 1516. He was given the manor house of Clos Lucé, near the royal Château d'Amboise, and a pension totalling 10,000 scudi. Leonardo drew plans for a castle town at Romorantin and made a mechanical lion that walked towards the king and opened its chest to reveal lilies. A visitor in October 1517 recorded that his right hand was paralytic, which may indicate why works such as the Mona Lisa were left unfinished.

After several months bedridden, Leonardo died at Clos Lucé on 2 May 1519 at the age of 67, possibly of a stroke. Vasari's story that the king held his head as he died may be legend rather than fact. His pupil Francesco Melzi was principal heir and executor, receiving his paintings, tools, library and papers; Salaì and a servant each received half of his vineyards. On 12 August 1519 he was interred in the Collegiate Church of Saint Florentin at the Château d'Amboise. The church was demolished in 1802, and the present location of his remains is unclear; a skeleton excavated in 1863 and reburied in the chapel of Saint Hubert in 1874 is only presumed to be his.
sections.legacy:
For the better part of four hundred years Leonardo's fame rested on his paintings. The Virgin and Child with Saint Anne influenced Michelangelo, Raphael and Andrea del Sarto, and he attracted a large following of imitators and students, among them Bernardino Luini and Giovanni Antonio Boltraffio. The Mona Lisa is regarded as the world's most famous painting and The Last Supper as the most reproduced religious painting of all time.

His notebooks, entrusted to Melzi for publication, proved too vast and idiosyncratic a task. After Melzi's death in 1570 they passed to his son Orazio, whose heirs sold them, and they were dispersed among collections that now include Windsor Castle, the Louvre, the Biblioteca Ambrosiana in Milan and the British Library. Material assembled by Melzi was published as A Treatise on Painting in 1651; according to Arasse it made Leonardo appear "the precursor of French academic thought on art". The anatomical drawings, had they been published, would have made a major contribution to medical science.

Tributes run from Baldassare Castiglione in 1528 and Vasari in 1568 to Hippolyte Taine, who in 1866 called him a universal genius "so incapable of fulfilment". Many historians regard him as the prime exemplar of the "Renaissance man"; the art historian Helen Gardner wrote that his mind and personality "seem to us superhuman". Experts still argue over attributions and search for recorded works that have never been found. For the 500th anniversary of his death the Louvre mounted the largest ever single exhibition of his work.

summary: Leonardo da Vinci trained in Florence under Verrocchio and worked for Ludovico Sforza in Milan, for Cesare Borgia, in Rome and finally for Francis I of France. He painted The Last Supper and the Mona Lisa and filled some 13,000 pages with notes and drawings on anatomy, machines and nature, which he never published. He died at Clos Lucé in 1519.
references: Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects (1550)
Leonardo da Vinci, A Treatise on Painting (1651)
Sigmund Freud, Leonardo da Vinci, A Memory of His Childhood
